## codegraph
# Codegraph — available (per-project; pass projectPath)

Codegraph is a SQLite knowledge graph of a codebase's symbols, edges, and
files: one `codegraph_explore` call returns the verbatim, line-numbered source
of the relevant symbols PLUS the call paths between them and a blast-radius
summary — replacing a grep + Read loop with one round-trip.

This server started somewhere with no `.codegraph/` of its own, so there is no
default project — but the tools are available and work **per project**:

- To query a project that HAS a `.codegraph/` index (e.g. a service inside a
  monorepo, or a second repo), pass its path as `projectPath` to
  `codegraph_explore` (and any other codegraph tool). Codegraph resolves the
  nearest `.codegraph/` at or above that path and answers from it — for as many
  projects as you like in one session.
- For a project with no `.codegraph/`, use your built-in tools (Read/Grep/Glob)
  for that project. Indexing is the user's decision — don't run it yourself, but
  if it comes up they can run `codegraph init` in a project to enable codegraph
  there (a new index is picked up live, no restart).


---
CodeGraph v1.6.2 is available (this server is running v1.4.1). Update with `codegraph upgrade`. This server keeps running the old version until the user upgrades — mention it when convenient; do not run the upgrade yourself.

## Reusable automation

When a shell command becomes long, fragile, or is likely to be used more than once,
prefer creating a small script under `scripts/` (or the repository's existing
automation directory) instead of repeatedly constructing long one-liners.

Reuse an existing script before creating a new one. Keep scripts parameterized
rather than hard-coding values specific to one invocation.

## Large log/output files

Before using `Read` on a large build or test-run output file (background task logs, CI output,
verbose test-harness dumps, etc.), filter it first with `grep`/`tail` via Bash for the lines
actually needed (e.g. failure markers, summary/result lines). Verbose per-iteration solver or
build spam in an otherwise-passing or unremarkable run adds little value and can consume a large
fraction of context if read wholesale. Only fall back to reading the raw file when the filtered
view doesn't answer the question, e.g. inspecting behavior right around a specific failure.

## Comment style in code/config diffs

Comments added to source or test files must read as normal repository documentation, not as a
narration of the investigation that produced them. Write the durable engineering rationale a
maintainer would want (what the code does and why, in general terms), not the debugging story
(specific timesteps/iteration counts observed in one run, "I found/confirmed" phrasing, or
session-specific values). If a concrete example is useful, prefer a generic illustrative one over
the exact number from a specific debugging session.

Avoid negating clauses that describe what was *not* done or contrast against an alternative
("rather than X", "instead of Y", "not a Z"), unless the contrast itself is the useful
information (e.g. explaining why an obvious-seeming alternative was rejected). State what the
code/comment/doc does directly instead of framing it against something it isn't.

## Answering questions in a turn that also does work

When a turn mixes questions with work to perform, do the work first and put the answers to the
questions in one clearly marked block at the end of the response, so they cannot be missed in
scrolled-past tool output or interleaved with progress reporting. Answer every question asked,
in the order asked, rather than folding some into the narration of the work.

## Hardware use

Never use more than 4 processes for building libraries/executables or for running tests.

## GitHub pull requests

Open every GitHub pull request you create as a draft (e.g. `gh pr create --draft`). Leave
marking it ready for review to the user.

## Pull/merge request dependencies

When writing a GitHub PR or GitLab MR description for a request with a known dependency on
another open PR/MR, make the first non-blank line of the description a dependency declaration in
the format the `pr-dependency-graph` skill parses, e.g.:

```
Depends on #4579, idaholab/moose#31000, petsc/petsc!9684
```

`#N` is a GitHub PR and `!N` a GitLab MR; bare forms refer to the same repository, and
`owner/repo#N` / `group/project!N` or a full URL refer to other repositories. Only the first line
is parsed, so keep any prose about the dependency below it.

# AGENTS.md

## Environment
- Ask the user if you need to load a MOOSE conda environment, and if so, what the name of the conda environment is
- If `./tmap8-opt` or `run_tests` throws an error, stop and ask the user
- Pre-commit hooks handle all formatting and input file validation on every `git commit` — do not invoke `clang-format`, `black`, or `hit format` manually
- `moose/framework/contrib/hit/hit check <file>.i` is available to validate input files during development — use it before committing

## Before writing any code or input file
- Browse `doc/content/` to understand documentation standards and existing patterns before starting work
- Before writing a new C++ class, look through existing MOOSE classes in the codebase to confirm expected syntax and patterns
- Documentation in `doc/content/` may not accurately reflect current code behavior — once you identify a class to use in an input file, find its C++ implementation and read it to confirm the class does what you expect before writing the input file

## C++ code
- Every new class requires a MOOSE TestHarness test in `test/tests/` before committing
- Every new class requires a MooseDocs page following existing TMAP8 doc structure
- Never hardcode physical parameters — first check if it is already defined in `doc/content/source/utils/TMAP8PhysicalConstants`, and if not available, expose everything through `addParam`
- Code is unit-agnostic; units live in input files only

## Input files
- Before writing an input file, look through existing MOOSE and TMAP8 classes to confirm object names and parameter syntax
